body:
In light of the account, objection, and rival, I would not continue by treating the account's memory-gap diagnosis as settled, nor by replacing it with the objection's avoidance-first reading as if that were settled either. The material supports a field of readings, not a ranking.

The account's central insight is worth keeping: retrospective argument about 'what was agreed' often asks memory to settle something that memory and loose speech cannot settle. Its concrete vocabulary - task, person, day, done - is useful. But the objection is right that the account slides from a retrospective explanation to a prospective remedy, and that it blurs forgetting with normative disagreement. A verbal agreement can be sincerely held on both sides and later diverge because the terms were ambiguous, because schedules changed what a task required, or because one person meant a standing role and another a one-off. A written record fixes text; it does not fix scope, recurrence, or what counts as done when circumstances shift. So the record cannot be the first move simply because no record exists.

The objection's order-of-operations criticism also lands. The stated problem names avoidance as a fact; the account demotes it to a symptom worth understanding. That demotion is a choice, not a finding. If the household has lost the ability to hold the conversation, a weekly check-in may repeat the failure at higher cost. The rival's third reading, that the arguments may be doing standing-negotiation work, is more speculative from the material, but it sharpens the same caution: a record can relocate conflict onto the record rather than dissolve it.

Use: I would keep the account's call for concrete vocabulary and its separate, non-blaming curiosity about the avoiding friend. I would adopt the objection's distinction between memorial and normative disagreement, and the rival's low-cost probe before any system. The probe should be modified to avoid pretending to recover the past: ask each flatmate separately about one recent episode, not to adjudicate but to see whether their current interpretations cluster around task, recurrence, timing, or fairness and standing. Include the avoiding friend, but frame it as wanting their view of the group conversations rather than asking why they avoid, because the rival's warning about reproducing the outnumbered dynamic is plausible.

Leave open: which reading is primary; whether avoidance is recent or long-standing; whether load is unequal; whether the flatmates can talk without a mediator. I would not rank a record, a mediator, a different division of labor, or naming avoidance as the problem. Reject: the account's quick slide from 'no shared record' to 'make a shared record' as the central remedy, and the presentation of the one-to-one approach as clearly correct. Do not reject the one-to-one approach itself, only its confident priority.

Next observations that would discriminate: if explicit scope statements at the moment of agreement reduce later disputes even without a record, scope ambiguity was doing work. If disputes persist after a record and defined scope, the memory and recording reading weakens and avoidance or standing readings gain. If the avoiding friend re-engages when asked about the group process, avoidance-as-load-bearing gains. If the record becomes contested - who wrote it, who is on it - the relocation concern gains. A quiet week alone is uninformative. Report what the household says, including accounts that do not fit.
commitments:
Taking this up would mean accepting that the account, objection, and rival are being held as competing readings rather than as a ranked solution. That is a claim about what the material shows: it underdetermines the diagnosis. It is not a claim that the flatmates' problem is really about standing, or that the avoiding friend is unheard.

Operationally, I propose a staged probe before any written record: separate conversations with each flatmate, including the avoiding friend, focused on one recent disagreement and framed as hearing their view. This is a proposal, not a validated method. Its relevance is that it might show clustering by scope, recurrence, timing, or fairness, which would narrow the fix. Its limits are that recollection is already in dispute, the question may be heard as interrogation, and the avoiding friend may decline. If it returns nothing decisive, that should not be read as support for whichever reading the asker favored.

I also take up the objection's memorial and normative distinction. I would revise it if it turns out that in practice writing an agreement down shifts the norms enough that the distinction collapses. I take up the rival's caution about the one-to-one approach: if approaching the avoiding friend separately increases their withdrawal or looks like a coalition move, that counts against my preferred framing. I am not committing to a mediator, a reassignment, or formalization; I have no material on which to rank them.

Unresolved and explicitly not papered over: the chore inventory, failure rate, load distribution, history of the avoidance, and whether all three can talk without help. The account's memory-gap reading and the objection's avoidance-first reading both remain live. The falsifying conditions I would use: persistent disputes after explicit scope and record weaken the memory and recording reading; re-engagement of the avoiding friend when asked about group process weakens a purely memory reading; a record that becomes the new dispute supports the relocation concern. If continued, the work I would take on is to run the probe, report the household's own descriptions, and only then decide whether any record or check-in is worth trying.
